runs.text: A “box” can be any class in a partition: a remainder, interval, color, or other category. Empty boxes are allowed.

blocks.tex: N\text{ objects in }k\text{ boxes}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{some box has at least }\left\lceil\frac Nk\right\rceil,\quad N\ge0,\ k\ge1

runs.text: The extremal principle begins by choosing an object with a largest or smallest relevant parameter and exploiting what extremality forces.
A useful contrapositive is: if every box has at most q objects, then there are at most kq objects total.

blocks.tex: N>kq\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{some box contains at least }q+1\text{ objects}

runs.text: Extremal choices often turn local inequalities into contradictions: choose the shortest distance, largest degree, earliest time, or smallest counterexample.

items.text: The boxes must cover every object and be mutually exclusive for the direct averaging statement.
Compute the ceiling only after identifying the correct number of boxes.
An extremal object exists automatically only in a finite nonempty set, or when a separate existence argument is supplied.
State what equality would mean; many sharp problems live exactly at the threshold.

runs.text: Assign 13 people to the 12 boxes given by their birth months. Since
at least two people share a birth month.

items.text: Pigeonhole proves existence but usually does not identify which box is crowded.
Overlapping categories are not boxes until each object is assigned unambiguously.
Choosing an extreme object is a starting point, not a proof; explicitly derive the forced property.
